passage:
Monday night.

Results came out. I missed the engineering entrance cutoff again, second time. Aadhya called, and I couldn't even speak properly.

Spent the evening lying on the roof, staring at the water tank, feeling like the biggest failure in the colony. Mummy left dinner outside my door. I didn't eat for a while.

Around eleven I finally opened my mock test sheets. And I saw it: maths was fine, physics was fine, chemistry was a disaster both years. It's not that I'm stupid. It's one subject I kept avoiding.

I'm going to try one more time. Not the same way. Chemistry first, every morning. I'll ask Aadhya's cousin for her notes.

I'm scared to fail again. But I'm more scared of never finding out.

Chetan

qa.q: Which subject did Chetan see was the weak one in both years?
qa.a: Chemistry.

qa.q: What does Chetan mean by being more scared of never finding out?
qa.a: Chetan is afraid of failing again, but would regret giving up more, so chooses to try instead of quitting.

qa.q: Which part of Chetan's new plan shows a lesson learned from the setback?
qa.a: Tackling chemistry first every morning, because it targets the actual reason for missing the cutoff.

qa.q: How might Aadhya feel when Chetan says they're trying again?
qa.a: Aadhya would probably be relieved and proud after hearing Chetan unable to speak on the phone, and glad to help with the notes.

grounding: A young adult's diary shows the writer finding the grit to try again after a major setback, with a smarter plan.

passage: At the village akhada, the red earth was still marked from yesterday's district bout. Vijay, twenty-one, had lost in the final round, pinned in under a minute in front of the whole village. That night he didn't go home. He sat by the pit until his coach, Omkar ustad, found him. "Shame?" asked Omkar. Vijay nodded. "Everyone saw." "Everyone saw you get there too," Omkar said. "Why did you lose?" Vijay thought. "I rushed. I got tired too early." "So?" Vijay stood up, brushed the earth off his legs. "So I train stamina. Morning runs to the canal and back." At dawn the next day, the village milkman saw him running past the fields, alone, his breath clouding in the cold.

qa.q: Where did the milkman see Vijay running at dawn?
qa.a: Past the fields.

qa.q: How was Vijay feeling after losing the bout?
qa.a: He felt ashamed because the whole village had watched him lose.

qa.q: What did Omkar's questions help Vijay do?
qa.a: They helped him find the real reason he lost and turn his shame into a concrete training plan.

qa.q: How might the milkman see Vijay running alone at dawn?
qa.a: He might be surprised and impressed that the boy who lost is already back at work.

grounding: Shows a young wrestler in a village finding the grit to train again after a public defeat.

passage: Javier, twenty-one, read the results on the board outside the training centre in Valencia twice before it sank in: failed again, the second time, by four points. He walked out and sat on the curb in the heat. His friend Chen, who had passed, sat down beside him without saying anything about his own result. 'I'm done,' Javier said. 'My uncle was right. I should just keep stacking boxes at the warehouse.' Chen waited. After a while Javier pulled the marked paper from his bag and looked at it properly. Almost all his mistakes were in the circuit calculations, not the practical. 'It's always the same section,' he muttered. That evening he taped the paper above his bed and asked Chen for his old calculation notes. The next exam was in March. He wrote the date on his hand.

qa.q: By how many points did Javier fail?
qa.a: Four points.

qa.q: Why did Javier say 'I'm done' at first?
qa.a: He felt crushed and discouraged after failing twice and was echoing his uncle's doubts.

qa.q: What turned Javier's setback into a plan?
qa.a: Looking closely at the marked paper showed his mistakes were in one section, which gave him a clear target to study.

qa.q: Why might Chen have said nothing about his own result?
qa.a: He sensed Javier's pain and chose to support him quietly rather than highlight his own pass.

grounding: Shows a young adult finding the grit to try again after a second failed exam.

passage: At the district sports hostel, the track lights came on at six. Sangeeta, twenty, had missed selection for the state relay team by one-tenth of a second, two weeks after coming back from a hamstring injury. For three days she didn't come to practice. On the fourth, Coach Manjula found her sitting in the stands. 'You can quit,' the coach said evenly. 'Nobody will blame you.' Sangeeta was quiet for a long time. 'If I quit now, the injury decides. I want to decide.' She laced her spikes. The first two starts were ugly; her leg felt stiff and her face burned with embarrassment in front of the juniors. On the third, she found her rhythm again. Coach Manjula wrote the next trial date on the whiteboard and underlined it twice.

qa.q: By how much did Sangeeta miss selection?
qa.a: By one-tenth of a second.

qa.q: What did Sangeeta mean by 'I want to decide'?
qa.a: She felt determined not to let the injury and setback end her running for her; she wanted to choose to keep trying.

qa.q: What was wise about the coach saying 'You can quit'?
qa.a: It removed pressure and let Sangeeta find her own reason to continue, which makes her determination stronger.

qa.q: How might the juniors see Sangeeta's ugly starts?
qa.a: They might notice her struggling, but also learn that senior athletes keep going after setbacks.

grounding: Illustrates a young athlete building the resolve to return to training after a painful setback.

passage:
Dear Nitin Sir,
I got the result today. I failed the second level of the accountancy exam again, by six marks. I cried the whole afternoon. For an hour I thought about giving up and taking any job. But I remembered what you said when I was your student: failure is information. So tonight I went through my paper. I lost most marks in taxation, the same as last time. I'm going to join the weekend batch you recommended and practise a full paper every Sunday. The next attempt is in six months. I'm scared, but I'm trying again.
Dolma

qa.q: By how many marks did Dolma fail?
qa.a: By six marks.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling during that hour of thinking about giving up?
qa.a: Dolma felt deeply discouraged and hurt after failing again.

qa.q: What did Dolma do that shows determination?
qa.a: Dolma studied the paper, found the weak area and made a specific plan for the next attempt.

qa.q: How might Nitin Sir feel reading this email?
qa.a: Moved and proud that a former student is using Sir's own words to try again.

grounding: Shows a young adult building the grit to try again after a significant exam setback.

passage: Swati, thanks for having me on your podcast. So, I'm Kiran, twenty-two, and my first business failed. I started a tiffin service in college with two friends. We had forty customers, then a food-safety complaint, and in two weeks we had none. We closed. I didn't cook for months. I felt like a fraud. Then my younger cousin asked me to make lunch for her hostel room, just once. I did, carefully, properly licensed this time. Now I have a small kitchen and thirty customers. Some days I'm still scared it'll all fall apart. But I'd rather try and fail than not try.

qa.q: How many customers does Kiran have now?
qa.a: Thirty customers.

qa.q: How did Kiran feel after the first business closed?
qa.a: Kiran felt like a fraud, ashamed and unwilling to cook for months.

qa.q: What turning point helped Kiran try again?
qa.a: A cousin's small request to cook lunch, which Kiran did carefully and properly licensed.

qa.q: How might Kiran's cousin see the new kitchen?
qa.a: Probably proud to have played a part, and happy to see Kiran succeed.

grounding: Shows a young adult building the determination to try again after a business failure.

passage: I'm Sahil, Kavitha's brother. Kavitha, twenty, missed selection for the national athletics camp by one place last year. She came home and didn't run for three weeks. Then one morning I heard her shoes on the stairs at five. She'd written a plan on the fridge: strength twice a week, video of every race, rest on Sundays. She found a new coach at the stadium. Some mornings she came back limping and silent. This year she made the camp. I don't know what kept her going on the bad days, but she never missed a five o'clock start.

qa.q: By how many places did Kavitha miss selection?
qa.a: By one place.

qa.q: What might Kavitha have felt during the three weeks she didn't run?
qa.a: She was probably devastated and discouraged after coming so close.

qa.q: What helped Kavitha succeed the second time?
qa.a: A clear written plan, a new coach and steady early training even on hard days.

qa.q: How does Sahil see his sister's comeback?
qa.a: He admires her discipline, though he can't know what kept her going.

grounding: Shows a young adult building grit to try again after a major sporting setback, seen by her brother.

passage:
June: Santosh, twenty-two, checked the civil services prelims result online in a Delhi cyber café. His roll number wasn't there. He walked home in the heat and lay on his bed for two days, not studying, not eating much.
July: His mentor, Vasudha Ma'am, called. "You were two marks short. Two. Come and see me." He went. They sat with his answer sheet and marked every mistake. He made a new timetable, with mock tests every Sunday.
Next May: Santosh sat the prelims again, hands steady this time. In the evening, he wrote in his notebook: "Whatever happens, I did it properly." He slept well for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: How many marks short was Santosh?
qa.a: Two marks.

qa.q: How did Santosh feel after the first result?
qa.a: He felt crushed and defeated, lying on his bed for two days.

qa.q: What helped Santosh try again?
qa.a: Vasudha Ma'am's call, going through every mistake and building a new timetable with weekly mock tests.

qa.q: How might Vasudha Ma'am feel about Santosh's second attempt?
qa.a: She would likely feel proud of his grit, whatever the result.

grounding: Over a year, a young man recovers from failing a major exam and builds the determination to try again.

passage: Siddharth Uncle cleaned his glasses. "Harish, you think one failure means you're done? At twenty-two, I started a small tiffin service with two friends. We cooked in my mother's kitchen, delivered on cycles. Within eight months, we'd lost everything we'd put in. One friend left. I cried in that kitchen, I won't lie. For a month I didn't want to see a tiffin box. Then my mother said, 'Did you learn nothing?' I had learned a lot: we'd priced too low, and delivered too far. So I tried again, alone, only offices within three kilometres. It was hard, and slow. That's the company I run now." Harish looked at his own laptop, where the rejected application was open. "So I just try again?" "You learn, and then you try again."

qa.q: How did they deliver the tiffins?
qa.a: On cycles.

qa.q: How did young Siddharth feel after the business failed?
qa.a: He felt crushed and discouraged, crying and not wanting to see a tiffin box for a month.

qa.q: What was the turning point in young Siddharth's story?
qa.a: His mother asking whether he'd learned anything, which made him see his mistakes and try again differently.

qa.q: How might the friend who left have seen young Siddharth's second attempt?
qa.a: That friend might feel surprised and perhaps a little regretful, seeing Siddharth succeed.

grounding: An uncle tells Harish how he recovered from a failed business at twenty-two and tried again.

passage: Uma, twenty-one, had sent out twenty internship applications and received twenty rejections. On the day the twenty-first came back no, her laptop screen cracked. She sat in the Kolkata college library on a borrowed computer, tired and furious. Her friend Arnab found her there. "Take a break?" "No." She pulled up a spreadsheet. "I'm finding out what's going wrong." They went through every application. Her cover letters were identical; she'd never named the company's actual work. "Okay," she said, jaw set. "New letters. Each one different." She wrote three that evening, until the library closed. Arnab walked her to the bus stop. "You're kind of scary right now." Uma laughed for the first time that week. "Good."

qa.q: How many rejections had Uma received before the twenty-first?
qa.a: Twenty.

qa.q: What was Uma feeling when she set her jaw?
qa.a: She felt frustrated but determined to fix what was going wrong.

qa.q: What change did Uma make after studying her rejections?
qa.a: Writing a different cover letter for each company, naming its actual work.

qa.q: How does Arnab see Uma's determination?
qa.a: Arnab is impressed and a little in awe, joking that she's scary.

grounding: Despite many rejections and a broken laptop, a young woman studies her mistakes and tries again.

passage:
Jasleen failed the civil services prelims for the second time. She sat in her small rented room in Delhi and didn't open a book for a week.
Her roommate Seema brought her parathas and left them on her desk without comment.
On the eighth day, Jasleen opened her answer sheets and made herself read every mistake. It hurt. Current affairs had pulled her down both times.
She wrote a new timetable: newspaper at seven, mock tests every Sunday, one full day off a week so she wouldn't burn out. She pinned it above her bed.
Seema read it. "Third time?"
"Third time." Jasleen's voice was steady. "And if not, I'll know I gave it everything."
Seema squeezed her shoulder and went to make chai.

qa.q: What pulled Jasleen down both times?
qa.a: Current affairs.

qa.q: How did Jasleen feel on the eighth day reading her mistakes?
qa.a: She felt hurt but steady and determined, making herself face every error.

qa.q: What makes Jasleen's new plan likely to help?
qa.a: It targets her weak area, adds regular mock tests, and includes a day off to avoid burning out.

qa.q: How does Seema seem to feel about Jasleen's week of silence?
qa.a: Seema seems concerned but patient, quietly bringing food and then supporting her new plan.

grounding: Shows a young adult recovering from a major setback and committing to try again.

passage:
"You're applying again?" Francis asked, stirring his tea.
"Yes." Lokesh closed the laptop. "Eleven rejections. I'm sending the twelfth."
"Don't you feel stupid?"
"Every time." Lokesh laughed. "But I read all the feedback. Three of them said my portfolio was weak on print design. So I did a print course."
"And if this one says no?"
"Then I'll know something else to fix."
Francis watched him. "Last year you gave up on football after one bad match."
"I know. That's why I'm doing this. I didn't like who I was when I gave up."
"Okay." Francis pushed his cup aside. "Show me the portfolio. I'll tell you what's boring."
"Brutal?"
"Brutal."

qa.q: How many rejections has Lokesh had?
qa.a: Eleven rejections.

qa.q: What does Lokesh's laugh suggest about how he feels?
qa.a: It suggests he feels embarrassed by the rejections but determined not to give up.

qa.q: What is Lokesh doing that makes trying again wise?
qa.a: He reads the feedback and fixes the weakness, like taking a print course, before applying again.

qa.q: How is Francis affected by Lokesh's attitude?
qa.a: Francis is surprised, remembering Lokesh quit football, and is moved to help review the portfolio.

grounding: Shows a young adult building grit to keep trying after repeated rejection.

passage:
I failed my nursing licence exam by four marks. I'm Jyoti. I remember reading the result in the hospital canteen and not being able to swallow.
For a week I told everyone I was done. I'd go back to my village, help in my uncle's shop, forget it.
My senior Nirmala didi found me on the stairs during a night shift. She didn't lecture. She said, "I failed twice. Look at me now." She was the ward in-charge.
Something in me got stubborn. I booked the next exam date that night. I studied at five in the morning before shifts, with her old notes.
I passed the second time. I still keep the first result slip in my drawer. It reminds me I can get up.

qa.q: By how many marks did Jyoti fail?
qa.a: Four marks.

qa.q: How did Jyoti feel on first reading the result?
qa.a: Jyoti felt crushed and defeated, unable to swallow and saying it was over.

qa.q: What was the turning point for Jyoti?
qa.a: Nirmala didi's story of failing twice sparked stubbornness, and Jyoti booked the next exam that night.

qa.q: How might Nirmala didi have felt seeing Jyoti pass?
qa.a: Nirmala didi would likely feel proud and happy that sharing her own failure helped.

grounding: A young adult recalls finding the grit to retake an exam after a painful failure.

passage:
Coach's note, district stadium, Saturday
Jeevan missed the fire-service physical last year by four seconds on the 1.6 km run. He didn't come to the ground for a month after. When he came back in January, he asked me to be honest about his form, and I was: his pacing fell apart after the second lap. He has been at the track at 5:30 every morning since, with his friend Tejas pacing him on a cycle. Two weeks ago he pulled a calf muscle and had to rest; I saw him sitting in the stands watching the others, jaw tight. He was back as soon as the physio cleared him. Today he ran it eleven seconds faster than last year. I've entered him for the next recruitment.

qa.q: By how many seconds did Jeevan miss the physical last year?
qa.a: By four seconds on the 1.6 km run.

qa.q: What does Jeevan's tight jaw in the stands suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt frustrated and restless at being sidelined, but determined not to give up.

qa.q: What helped Jeevan try again after the setback?
qa.a: Asking for honest feedback, training steadily with a pacing partner, and resting the injury properly until the physio cleared him.

qa.q: How does the coach see Jeevan's comeback?
qa.a: The coach respects his steady effort and shows faith in him by entering him for the next recruitment.

grounding: Shows a young adult rebuilding after failing a recruitment test and an injury, observed by his coach.
